Context/Background:
Tumor-infiltrating B cells play a significant role in tumor development, progression, and prognosis, yet a comprehensive classification system is lacking. To address this gap, we present a pan-cancer single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) atlas of tumor-infiltrating B and plasma cells across a large sample cohort. 

We isolated B cells and plasma cells from 15 studies spanning 7 cancer types as data sources. After applying batch correction and integrating the data, we removed low-quality cells and determined the optimal number of clusters. Using standard Seurat methods for integration, clustering, and differential expression analysis, we confirmed the absence of batch effects, with no study- or cancer type-specific clusters. 

We employed a graph-based clustering method to identify TIL-Bs with recurring phenotypes, uncovering a total of 10 clusters. Step one of cluster annotation used canonical markers like CD19 and MS4A1 (CD20), which are prevalent throughout B cell development but decline in plasma cells. Markers such as CD38, JCHAIN, and SDC1 (CD138) are prominent in plasma cells, but less so in earlier stages. This revealed four B cell clusters, two intermediate clusters with proliferative and germinal center (GC) features, and four plasma cell clusters.
Prompt: Based on upregulated pathways and differentially expressed markers in each cluster, assign functional phenotypes to each of the 2 intermediate clusters (clusters 5-6).  Provide a discussion of the reasoning behind cluster assignments, highlighting important genes and pathways where relevant.

Introduction/Context  
A pan-cancer single-cell RNA-seq atlas of tumor-infiltrating B and plasma cells was assembled from 15 studies across seven cancer types (S1535610824003593). After batch-corrected integration (Seurat), ten transcriptional clusters were defined; clusters 5–6 are intermediate (“transitional”) B cell states. Canonical B cell (CD19, MS4A1) and plasma cell (CD38, SDC1) markers stratify early-stage B cells from mature plasma cells; the intermediate clusters were not cancer- or study-specific. The two intermediate clusters lacked canonical plasma markers but showed distinct pathway activations and marker expression patterns.  

Keywords  
• Proliferation (cell cycle, mitosis)  
• Translation / Ribosome biogenesis  
• Germinal center (GC) / antigen presentation  
• Endosomal–lysosomal transport  
• Mitochondrial biogenesis  

Candidate Genes  
• STMN1, HMGB2, TFAM (cluster 5)  
• RGS13, MS4A1, HLA-DMB, BIN1 (cluster 6)  

Functional Phenotypes & Rationale  

Cluster 5 (Intermediate) – “Proliferative B cells”  
• Key markers upregulated: STMN1 (avg_log2FC 3.17; pct.1 = 0.894), HMGB2 (3.14; 0.904) and TFAM (2.58; 0.405), indicating chromatin remodeling and mitochondrial biogenesis.  
• GSEA (MSigDB Hallmark) revealed strong positive NES for E2F Targets (NES 4.74; leading genes STMN1, HMGB2, MCM7, RFC1, TUBB), G2-M Checkpoint (NES 4.05; STMN1, ORC6, MKI67, UBE2C, PTTG1), and Mitotic Spindle (NES 2.29; SMC4, BIRC5, TOP2A, CEP57, AURKB). Downregulated Hallmarks included Adipogenesis (NES –2.92) and Oxidative Phosphorylation (–2.10).  
• KEGG pathways upregulated: Ribosome (NES 2.89; RPL10A, RPL39, RPS27, RPS17, UBA52), Cell cycle (2.68; CCNA2, MCM7, CDK1, CDC20, PLK1), Oocyte meiosis (2.37; SMC3, CDC20, CCNB2, CDK1). TCA cycle (–2.51) and Endocytosis (–2.43) were down.  
• GO Biological Processes up: Cytoplasmic Translation (NES 3.47; RPL/RPS family), Macromolecule Biosynthetic Process (3.15), Peptide Biosynthetic Process (3.11). Down: Negative Regulation of Proteasomal Protein Catabolism (–2.80).  
Rationale: The convergence of cell-cycle checkpoints, mitosis, ribosomal biogenesis, and peptide synthesis, alongside chromatin-remodeling factors (HMGB2) and mitochondrial TFAM, indicates a highly proliferative transitional B cell population.  

Cluster 6 (Intermediate) – “Germinal-center–like / antigen-processing B cells”  
• Top differentially expressed markers: RGS13 (avg_log2FC 1.92; pct.1 = 0.668), MS4A1 (CD20; 1.81; 0.948), HLA-DMB (1.67; 0.793), HLA-DPA1 (1.60; 0.939), LCK (1.71; 0.433), LAT2 (1.74; 0.663). RGS13 is a canonical germinal-center marker.  
• ORA on upregulated genes (p_adj < 0.05) highlighted GO terms:  
  – Endosome to Lysosome Transport (GO:0008333; p_adj = 0.0081; BIN1, DENND3)  
  – Lysosomal Transport (GO:0007041; 0.0107; BIN1, DENND3)  
  – Lipid Droplet Disassembly / Positive Regulation of Triglyceride Sequestering (GO:1905691/GO:0010889; p_adj = 0.0228; PLIN3)  
  – Regulation of Rab Protein Signal Transduction (GO:0032483; 0.0228; DENND3)  
  – Negative Regulation of Amyloid-β Formation / APP Catabolism (GO:1902430/GO:1902959; 0.0265; BIN1)  
Rationale: High expression of RGS13 and MHC II genes, together with enrichment in endosomal/lysosomal trafficking and lipid droplet remodeling, mirrors germinal-center B cells’ “antigen‐processing” machinery and trafficking through lysosomal compartments for peptide loading.  

Discussion  
Cluster 5 cells exhibit a robust proliferative signature—upregulation of E2F targets, G2-M checkpoint, mitotic spindle and ribosomal biogenesis pathways—consistent with actively cycling transitional B cells exiting germinal centers to differentiate (e.g., into plasmablasts). Downregulation of oxidative metabolism and adipogenesis suggests a metabolic shift prioritizing biomass accumulation over catabolism. In contrast, cluster 6 balances canonical GC markers (RGS13, CD20, HLA-DMB) with enhanced endosomal/lysosomal trafficking and lipid-droplet turnover, reflecting antigen capture, processing, and presentation functions typical of germinal-center B cells prior to proliferation or differentiation.  

These assignments link cluster 5 to a “proliferative” intermediate and cluster 6 to a “germinal-center–like / antigen-processing” intermediate phenotype.
